title: Chip War
author: Chris Miller
comment: The book I hand people who ask why chips keep turning up in foreign policy. Miller's case is that where you can make something decides who holds the leverage.

title: The Innovator's Dilemma
author: Clayton M. Christensen
comment: I keep coming back to this one. Christensen's point is that good companies fail not by doing the wrong things, but by doing the right ones for the customers they already have.

title: AI Superpowers
author: Kai-Fu Lee
comment: Lee's argument that implementation beats invention has aged well — and from where I sat in Beijing, the chapters on execution speed read less like prediction than description.

title: The China Questions
author: Jennifer Rudolph & Michael Szonyi (eds.)
comment: Not one argument but many — China scholars disagreeing with each other in a single volume. Useful precisely because it refuses to reduce the country to one storyline.

title: Wenn China angreift
author: Andreas Fulda
comment: A 2027 Taiwan scenario followed all the way through to its economic consequences. The chapters on German exposure are the ones I'd give anyone who thinks this is a distant problem.

title: Prediction Machines
author: Ajay Agrawal, Joshua Gans & Avi Goldfarb
comment: The most useful reframing I know: AI as a fall in the cost of prediction. See it that way and which tasks it changes — and which it doesn't — stops being guesswork.

title: Human + Machine
author: Paul R. Daugherty & H. James Wilson
comment: The 'missing middle' — the work that only exists when people and machines do it together. It's the part of the automation debate that usually gets skipped.

title: A World Appears
author: Michael Pollan
comment: Pollan spends the whole book asking what consciousness actually is and never pretends to land it. That patience is the point — we are busy building machines that act intelligent without knowing what experiencing anything even means.
